c.tagline: Sahelian river capital of music, markets, and the mighty Niger.

taxi.fareNote: Fares are negotiated before the ride, not metered; shared green taxis follow set routes while 'taxi déplacement' can be chartered privately for a higher fixed price.

emergency.note: Fire brigade: 18. Response times can be slow; the U.S. Embassy recommends Clinique Pasteur or Clinique Farako for serious medical issues. Mali is under a Level 4 (Do Not Travel) advisory due to terrorism, kidnapping, and crime.

hood_landmark.Quartier du Fleuve: Palais de la Culture Amadou Hampâté Bâ, Bamako

avoid.reason: Most governments advise against all travel to Mali; avoid any travel beyond the city limits and steer clear of government, military and crowd-gathering sites where attacks and protests occur.
Armed robbery and carjacking rise sharply after dark — avoid nighttime movement, use vetted drivers, and stay away from demonstrations.

hood_desc: Bamako's modern business and diplomatic quarter, with wide paved avenues, embassies, banks, and the city's newest hotels and restaurants; suits business travelers and those wanting reliable amenities.
Central, leafy, and relatively walkable, home to the racecourse, UN offices, and a concentration of restaurants and bars popular with expats and NGO workers; a good all-round base.

A quieter university-district neighborhood on the Niger River's south bank, linked to downtown by the Pont des Martyrs; long the go-to base for backpackers and overlanders thanks to budget guesthouses.
The historic riverside core of the city, with government buildings, the Palais de la Culture, the National Museum, and the city's oldest grand hotels; central for sightseeing on foot or by taxi.
A commercial, artisan-market riverside area on the road toward Koulikoro, near Point G hill; less polished but atmospheric, with a couple of long-standing riverside hotels.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; use bottled or treated water.

sys.n: STUB (Société des Transports Urbains de Bamako)

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or a fare collector aboard the minibus; there is no electronic ticketing system. SOTRAMA fares are very low (roughly 25-50 cents) and set per route segment rather than metered.
transit.hours: Roughly 6am-9pm; service thins out after dark and there is little to no formal night transit, so taxis are used after dark.
transit.note: SOTRAMA green-and-yellow minibuses are the backbone of transit, supplemented by shared and private taxis; STUB buses run a smaller formal network.

train: Bamako-Kayes line (freight, very limited/irregular passenger service)
bus: intercity coaches (Bani Transport, Somatra Sarl, Binke Transport) to regional cities
ferry: Seasonal pirogue and ferry crossings of the Niger River

tip.r: Not traditionally expected; rounding up or a small tip (5-10%) is appreciated at upscale restaurants and hotels but not required elsewhere.
